That is why we must enforce the corporate death penalty.

The corporate death penalty is not a slogan. It is not revenge. It is a legal and moral principle: when a corporation persistently violates the public trust, its charter should be revoked, its privileges withdrawn, and its existence brought to an end. Because a corporation is not a natural person. It is a creation of law. It exists because the public permits it to exist. And when it uses that permission to repeatedly harm the public, it forfeits its right to continue.

We do not allow individuals to commit crimes indefinitely just because they are wealthy. We do not tell repeat offenders, “Pay a fee and carry on.” Yet that is too often exactly what happens when powerful corporations break the law. They pollute rivers and pay a fine. They steal wages and pay a settlement. They deceive consumers and issue a press release. They violate safety rules, workers are injured or killed, and executives move on with bonuses intact.

This is not accountability. This is permission.

A fine that a corporation can easily absorb is not justice—it is a price tag. A settlement without admission of wrongdoing is not justice—it is a bargain. A promise to “do better” after years of illegal conduct is not justice—it is public relations.

Justice requires consequences strong enough to change behavior. And for the worst repeat corporate offenders, the consequence must be dissolution.

We must remember: corporations receive extraordinary benefits from society. Limited liability. Access to courts. Protection of contracts. Public infrastructure. Educated workers. Police and fire protection. Trade systems. Tax advantages. Legal recognition. These are not natural rights. They are privileges granted because corporations are supposed to serve lawful, productive purposes.

When a corporation becomes a repeat offender—when its business model depends on deception, exploitation, corruption, pollution, or abuse—it has broken the bargain. It has taken the benefits of society while attacking the society that sustains it.

And no institution should be too big to obey the law.

Some will say this idea is too radical. But what is truly radical is allowing corporations to repeatedly harm communities and still continue operating as if nothing happened. What is radical is a system where a person can be jailed for stealing groceries, while a corporation can steal millions in wages and face no existential consequence. What is radical is telling ordinary people to respect the law while telling corporate giants they can negotiate around it.

That is not the rule of law. That is rule by wealth.

The corporate death penalty would send a clear message: if your company repeatedly endangers the public, defrauds people, corrupts government, abuses workers, or poisons the environment, you do not get endless chances. You do not get to hide behind lawyers and lobbyists forever. You do not get to buy your way out of accountability.

You can lose your charter. You can lose your license to operate. You can be dismantled.

And let us be clear: dismantling a criminal corporation does not mean abandoning workers or communities. A just corporate death penalty must protect employees, pensions, consumers, and the public. Assets can be transferred. Essential services can continue under responsible ownership, public control, cooperatives, or restructured entities. Workers should not pay the price for executive lawlessness. Communities should not be punished for corporate misconduct.

The goal is not chaos. The goal is justice.

The goal is to remove the shield that lets repeat corporate offenders survive every scandal, every lawsuit, every disaster, and every betrayal. The goal is to make clear that corporations exist to serve society—not to dominate it, exploit it, or stand above it.

Imagine what this would mean.

Imagine executives sitting in boardrooms knowing that repeated illegal conduct could destroy the company, not just dent quarterly profits. Imagine shareholders demanding real compliance because the future of the corporation is at stake. Imagine regulators with the power to do more than issue fines. Imagine communities knowing that the law has teeth, that their lives and health and labor matter more than a corporation’s balance sheet.

That is the kind of accountability democracy demands.

We must build a system where corporate charters are treated as public trusts, not blank checks. We must empower attorneys general, courts, and regulators to pursue charter revocation against repeat offenders. We must require transparent records of corporate violations. We must escalate penalties for repeated misconduct. We must hold executives personally accountable when they direct, conceal, or profit from illegal activity. And when a corporation proves, through its own repeated actions, that it cannot or will not obey the law, we must have the courage to end it.

Because fairness means nothing if the powerful are exempt.

Accountability means nothing if consequences never reach the top.

Justice means nothing if the law bends before wealth.

The corporate death penalty is not about being anti-business. It is about being pro-law, pro-worker, pro-community, pro-democracy, and pro-justice. Honest businesses should welcome it, because they should not have to compete against corporations that cut corners, break laws, exploit workers, and poison communities to increase profits. A fair market requires rules. A just society requires enforcement. A democracy requires that no private power become untouchable.

So let us reject the lie that corporations are invincible. Let us reject the idea that repeated harm can be washed away with fines and apologies. Let us reject a two-tiered system of justice—one for the rich and powerful, and another for everyone else.

If a corporation repeatedly breaks the law, it should lose the privilege of existing.

Not someday. Not in theory. Not only in the most extreme case after decades of delay.

But as a real, enforceable consequence.

Because the law must have meaning.

Because communities deserve protection.

Because workers deserve dignity.

Because democracy must be stronger than corporate power.

And because justice demands that when any institution—no matter how wealthy, no matter how connected, no matter how large—repeatedly violates the public trust, we have the courage to say:

Your privilege is revoked. Your charter is dissolved. Your time is over.

That is accountability.

That is fairness.

That is justice.

The Corporate Death Penalty: Restoring Real Accountability

Corporations in the modern economy enjoy the legal fiction of personhood while evading the most basic consequence any actual person faces for repeated serious crime: the end of their existence. They pollute rivers, defraud millions, kill customers through defective products, launder money for cartels, and rig markets—then pay fines that amount to a rounding error on quarterly earnings. The result is a predictable cycle: headline-grabbing settlement, public relations apology, modest stock dip, and business as usual. This is not accountability; it is rent-seeking with extra steps. The only remedy capable of changing incentives at scale is the corporate death penalty—the mandatory, court-ordered dissolution and liquidation of companies found guilty of repeated or egregious violations of law.

The core problem is structural. Contemporary corporate penalties are calibrated to the logic of deterrence through cost internalization. In theory, a fine equal to the expected harm plus a premium should make misconduct unprofitable. In practice, it functions as a licensing fee for illegal behavior. Major banks paid roughly $150 billion in fines and settlements after the 2008 financial crisis yet continued operating with the same incentive structures and, in many cases, the same leadership class. Purdue Pharma’s role in the opioid epidemic killed hundreds of thousands; the company was restructured and its owners largely protected through bankruptcy maneuvers. Boeing’s systematic undermining of safety protocols contributed to the 737 MAX disasters; the company remains one of America’s largest contractors. BP’s Deepwater Horizon spill devastated the Gulf of Mexico; it paid fines and moved on. These are not aberrations. They are the predictable outcome when the worst possible sanction is “pay a fraction of the profits you made while breaking the law.”

A corporate death penalty changes the calculus from marginal cost to existential risk. Executives and boards would face a genuine survival constraint. The knowledge that three strikes—or one catastrophic strike—could result in the forced unwinding of the enterprise, the cancellation of the corporate charter, and the distribution of assets to creditors and victims creates powerful preventive incentives. Corporate counsel would suddenly treat regulatory compliance and criminal law as survival issues rather than negotiation points. Risk management departments would gain real authority instead of serving as theatrical compliance theater. Boards would think twice before promoting executives who deliver short-term numbers through creative rule-breaking.

Critics predict economic Armageddon. They claim innocent employees and shareholders would suffer, innovation would be chilled, and markets would collapse without their favorite corporate villains. These objections collapse under scrutiny.

First, shareholders are not helpless widows. Institutional investors and diversified funds hold the vast majority of public company stock. They can and should bear the cost of betting on criminals. The prospect of total loss would force them to engage in meaningful oversight—the kind of active governance that “stakeholder capitalism” rhetoric promises but rarely delivers. Second, employees of dissolved companies do not vanish. The productive assets, talent, and market demand do not disappear. Other firms, often more ethical competitors, acquire the viable pieces through liquidation. The history of antitrust breakups and bankruptcy reorganizations shows that economic activity continues; what changes is the concentration of unaccountable power. Third, the alternative to dissolution is not preservation at all costs. It is the continued existence of organizations that have proven, through repeated court findings, that they are incapable of lawful operation. If a human being commits serial violent felonies, we do not fine them and hope for the best. We remove them from society. The corporate analogue is dissolution.

Implementation is straightforward and requires no constitutional revolution. Courts already possess equitable powers to revoke corporate charters in extreme cases, a power some states have held since the 19th century. Congress could enact a federal standard defining “egregious or repeated illegal behavior” to include patterns of criminal convictions, massive regulatory violations causing widespread harm, or demonstrated systemic evasion of law through subsidiary structures and regulatory arbitrage. The process would include full due process: jury trials where appropriate, clear standards of liability, appeals, and a graduated system that begins with monitors, heavy fines, and management bans before reaching the ultimate sanction. Judges could appoint receivers to manage orderly wind-downs, ensuring critical functions (if any) continue under new ownership while the offending entity ceases to exist.

The alternative to this reform is the status quo: corporations as immortal, amoral profit engines that treat law as an input cost. This is incompatible with the rule of law and with the original understanding of the corporate form. Corporations were granted limited liability and perpetual life as privileges, not rights, precisely because they were expected to serve the public interest. When they instead become engines of concentrated harm, the state retains both the right and the duty to revoke the privilege.

Opponents who clutch pearls about “killing companies” should remember that markets kill companies every single day through competition, disruption, and bankruptcy. We simply propose adding law-breaking to the list of mortal sins. The corporate death penalty is not radical. It is the logical extension of treating corporations as legal persons. If they want the rights, they must accept the consequences—including capital punishment for the corporate form.

The era of polite fines and “lessons learned” press releases must end. Real deterrence requires real fear. For corporations that repeatedly demonstrate contempt for the societies that grant them existence, the only credible sanction is the end of that existence. The corporate death penalty is not vengeance. It is the minimum requirement for any legal system that claims to apply equally to all persons, fictional or not. Anything less is performative governance in service of the powerful.

It is time to stop pretending that trillion-dollar entities are too big to fail and too big to jail. Some of them are simply too big to tolerate.

Prompt:
Explain the reasons and supposed benefits of adopting a policy that enforces a corporate death penalty, where corporations engaging in serious or repeated illegal acts are forcibly dissolved, from a neutral, factual perspective.
Model Response:

Corporate Death Penalty (Revocation of Corporate Charter/Dissolution)

The "corporate death penalty" refers to a policy under which the state revokes a corporation's legal existence—its charter or equivalent—for serious violations of law or repeated, egregious offenses. Upon dissolution, the entity's assets are liquidated, creditors paid according to priority, and remaining value typically distributed or sold, with the corporate entity ceasing to operate as a going concern. This is distinct from bankruptcy, fines, or restructuring; the corporation is forcibly put out of business by government action.

Legal and Historical Basis

Corporations are legal fictions created by state charter or registration. Under traditional corporate law (both Anglo-American common law and civil law systems), the state retains the power to revoke that franchise for abuse.

  • Early U.S. practice (late 18th to early 20th century): Corporate charters were often granted for limited purposes and time periods. States routinely revoked charters for exceeding authorized powers (ultra vires), monopolistic practices, or corruption. Examples include revocations against railroads, banks, and manufacturing companies by states such as New York, Pennsylvania, and Ohio.
  • Modern remnants: Many U.S. state corporation statutes and the federal government still retain dissolution authority for fraud, repeated violations, or public harm (e.g., antitrust laws, banking regulations, or state attorney general actions). The FTC and DOJ have occasionally sought breakup or dissolution in extreme monopoly cases (Standard Oil in 1911 was broken into pieces; recent calls have targeted large tech firms). Similar provisions exist in the UK (Companies Act), India (Companies Act, 2013), and EU competition law.
  • Precedent for escalation: When civil and criminal penalties repeatedly fail to change behavior, proponents argue the logical endpoint is removal of the legal privilege to exist as a limited-liability entity.

Reasons Offered for the Policy

Proponents, including some legal scholars, consumer advocates (e.g., Ralph Nader's associated work), historians of corporate law (e.g., Thom Hartmann), and certain policymakers, advance these core arguments:

  1. Corporations as Creatures of the State: Since the state grants the privileges of limited liability, perpetual life, asset shielding, and contract rights, it can withdraw them when those privileges are used to cause systematic harm. This is framed as enforcement of the original charter contract rather than radical redistribution.

  2. Failure of Current Sanctions: Fines and settlements are frequently treated as a cost of doing business. Empirical patterns show repeat offenders across industries:

    • Major banks paid tens of billions in fines after the 2008 financial crisis yet continued similar practices.
    • Pharmaceutical companies (e.g., Purdue Pharma and others in the opioid crisis) paid large penalties while sales continued.
    • Automotive firms (Volkswagen emissions fraud, General Motors ignition switch scandal, Boeing 737 MAX issues) incurred fines but retained core operations. Proponents argue monetary penalties are discounted by probability of detection, diffuse shareholder ownership, and executive incentives tied to short-term results. Dissolution raises the penalty to existential level.

  3. Preventing Recidivism and "Too Big to Jail": When wrongdoing is embedded in corporate culture, strategy, or profit model, incremental penalties often fail. Dissolution removes the specific legal vehicle and management team with a track record of serious illegality, preventing continued operation under the same brand, culture, and incentive structures.

  4. Asymmetry Between Natural Persons and Legal Persons: Individuals can lose their liberty or, in some jurisdictions, their lives for serious crimes. Corporations currently face only financial consequences even after causing mass harm (environmental disasters, widespread fraud, deadly products). The policy seeks proportional accountability for artificial entities.

  5. Democratic Control Over Economic Power: Chartering is a public act. Persistent violation of criminal or regulatory law is seen as a breach of the public license to operate, justifying revocation in the same way professional licenses or operating permits are revoked for individuals or smaller businesses.

Supposed Benefits Claimed by Advocates

Advocates claim the following outcomes, presented here as arguments rather than empirically proven results (empirical studies of modern widespread use are limited because the policy is rarely applied to large firms):

  • Stronger Deterrence: The credible threat of non-existence is expected to increase investment in compliance, ethical culture, and risk management at the board and C-suite level, particularly for high-harm activities (environmental violations, consumer fraud, systemic financial risk).

  • Protection of the Public: Removes organizations that have demonstrated they repeatedly externalize massive costs onto society (pollution, defective products, financial contagion) rather than allowing them to continue under new management or reorganized forms.

  • Reallocation of Resources: Liquidated assets, intellectual property, and physical plant can be sold to new owners without the prior tainted governance culture. This is argued to be more efficient than perpetual fines paid to government while the harmful entity persists.

  • Improved Corporate Governance Norms: Boards would face personal career risk for allowing legal violations that threaten the firm's existence, tightening oversight. Insurance markets and lenders would likely price the risk of dissolution into their terms, creating market discipline.

  • Restoration of the Charter Concept: Returns corporate law closer to its historical understanding that the corporation is a tool serving public purposes, not an unlimited private right. This is said to reduce regulatory capture and political power of chronic offenders.

  • Equity with Small Entities: Small businesses and sole proprietors routinely lose their ability to operate for serious or repeated violations (license revocation, debarment). Extending similar logic to large corporations is framed as rule-of-law consistency rather than special treatment for size.

In practice, implementation would require clear statutory criteria (e.g., felony convictions, pattern of settlements exceeding a threshold, harm to public health/safety), due process protections, judicial oversight, and rules for handling employees, pensions, and innocent shareholders. Proponents generally limit the penalty to the most severe or chronic cases rather than routine regulatory infractions.

This framework represents the main substantive arguments made in legal, historical, and policy literature supporting the concept.

Maybe it's you.

When a human being commits a series of murders through negligence or malice, society does not simply fine them and let them walk away. They are imprisoned or executed. The current system of corporate punishment is fundamentally broken because it treats financial penalties as a cost of doing business rather than deterring wrongdoing. Consider the case of Volkswagen, which deliberately installed "defeat devices" to cheat emissions tests. It paid over $20 billion in fines and settlements—but in the same year, it reported $16.7 billion in net profit. For investors, the cost was merely noise in a spreadsheet. Similar patterns repeat across industries: BP’s $65 billion in costs from the Deepwater Horizon disaster did not prevent future environmental negligence; it barely dented its $150 billion market capitalization. Pharma giants like Purdue Pharma paid $8.3 billion for their role in the opioid crisis but continued operations until the company was dissolved in bankruptcy—a process divorced from criminal accountability. These fines are arithmetic exercises for corporations, not consequences. As Nobel laureate economist Joseph Stiglitz observed, "When the price of wrongdoing is less than the profit to be made, wrongdoing will happen." The system is designed to fail.

Why? Because limited liability—the legal shield protecting shareholders from personal responsibility—turns corporate crime into a risk-free venture. Executives gamble with other people’s money, knowing that even if they lose, the corporation’s assets (not their personal wealth) absorb the blow. Dissolution changes this equation entirely. It terminates the entity itself, forcing shareholders to bear the total loss of their investment. No more hiding behind corporate structures; the true cost of reckless behavior becomes catastrophic. If a corporation fleeces pension funds through systematic fraud—like Enron did—dissolution ensures that the same investors who enabled its growth through capital support also lose everything. This is not collective punishment; it is rational risk allocation. When the potential consequence is existential, boards and executives will enforce ethical controls with ferocious urgency. Shareholders, the ultimate beneficiaries of corporate success, will lose all incentive to tolerate greed. As legal scholar Elizabeth Pollman argues, "Ending the corporation is the only way to make the risk of corporate malfeasance feel real to those who control it."

Critics will claim dissolution punishes innocent employees and communities. This is a red herring. First, dissolution is reserved only for entities proven guilty of repeated or egregious crimes—such as deliberate pollution causing public health crises, systematic wage theft, or explosive fraud. These are not minor oversights; they are the policies of the corporation itself. When Lehman Brothers collapsed in 2008, 25,000 employees lost jobs overnight—but there was no call to "save the company" because it was morally bankrupt. Dissolution for criminal corporations is no different: it is simply the consistent application of consequences. Moreover, this policy would incentivize swift government intervention to retrain workers and transition communities, as seen in model programs like the Economic Development Administration’s "just transition" initiatives for coal-dependent regions. Others will decry "government overreach," but this ignores the fundamental social contract. Corporations do not exist in a vacuum; they are chartered by the state and granted extraordinary privileges—like perpetual existence, free speech rights, and limited liability—that no natural person enjoys. In return, society expects them to operate within the law. When a corporation becomes a moral and legal outlaw—functioning as a "sovereign threat," as philosopher Michael Sandel calls it—it forfeits its right to exist. The state already revokes the licenses of abusive charities, nonprofits, or professional associations; why should for-profit entities be held to a lower standard? As the U.S. Supreme Court acknowledged in United States v. Philadelphia National Bank (1963), corporations derive their existence from "public grants," and thus society retains the power to "revoke" them when they violate the public interest. To demand the rights of personhood while rejecting accountability is the height of hypocrisy.

The alternative is not "good" corporations—it is a further erosion of public trust and a permission structure for further harm. We have seen this with Tech: Facebook (Meta) ignored violence incitement on its platforms even after congressional hearings, merited by its lax oversight and algorithmic amplification of hate. When fines fail, only dissolution can reset the game. Imagine a Tesla found guilty of systemic safety deception that causes preventable deaths: dissolution would eliminate the profit incentive to cut corners, forcing the industry to rebuild with safety as its core value. It is not about vengeance; it is about societal self-defense.

Society does not tolerate human sociopaths who repeatedly endanger others. Why should we tolerate corporate sociopaths? The corporate death penalty is not a radical idea—it is the logical culmination of the principle that privileges require responsibility. When a corporation becomes a persistent vector of harm, it is not enough to slap its wrist and fine it into oblivion. We must delete it. Only then can we force real accountability, restore dignity to the market, and ensure that the creation of wealth never comes at the cost of human dignity or ecological survival. The state granted life; the state must have the power to take it back. Our future depends on it.

The Corporate Death Penalty: Neutral, Factual Explanation

The term "corporate death penalty" refers to a theoretical legal policy in which a corporation is forcibly dissolved (i.e., legally terminated as an entity) by judicial or regulatory order due to serious or repeated illegal acts. No country currently implements this as a standard policy for corporations. It remains a debated concept, not an established practice. Below, I describe the rationale, supposed benefits, and counterarguments purely from a factual perspective—without endorsing or rejecting the idea—based on legal scholarship, regulatory history, and economic theory.

Core Concept

  • Definition: A dissolution order would legally terminate the corporation’s existence, halting all operations, liquidating assets, and rendering the entity incapable of conducting business. Distinctions from other actions:
    • Not bankruptcy: Bankruptcy involves restructuring or asset liquidation under bankruptcy laws, but the entity may continue in new form. Dissolution ends the legal personhood entirely.
    • Not fines or regulatory sanctions: These impose monetary penalties or operational restrictions but do not eliminate the corporation.
  • Scope: Typically proposed only for willful, egregious violations (e.g., intentional environmental poisoning, fatal fraud causing widespread harm, or persistent criminal conduct) where lesser penalties (fines, injunctions) are deemed ineffective.

Arguments Cited by Proponents

  1. Enhanced Deterrence:

    • Theory: Corporations operate primarily to maximize shareholder value. If the risk of total dissolution outweighs the potential profits from illegal activity, executives and boards would prioritize compliance.
    • Evidence: Behavioral economics shows that severe, irreversible consequences deter risk-taking. For example, studies (e.g., Cass & Rendleman, 2001) suggest that high-impact penalties reduce misconduct more effectively than repetitive fines. Regulators (e.g., the U.S. SEC) have noted that fines often fail as deterrents when corporations view them as "the cost of doing business."

  2. Proportional Justice for Severe Harm:

    • Theory: When corporations cause mass harm (e.g., poisoning communities, destabilizing financial systems), only dissolution provides a punishment commensurate with the crime. Fines are insufficient if a corporation remains operational post-violation.
    • Historical Context: In rare cases like United States v. Arthur Andersen (2002), an accounting firm was dissolved after aiding Enron’s fraud, though the conviction was later overturned. Proponents argue this case illustrates dissolution as a tool for "corporate accountability" where punishment should match the scale of harm.

  3. Systemic Risk Mitigation:

    • Theory: Dissolving corporations that persistently endanger public safety or financial stability (e.g., banks whose misconduct triggered the 2008 crisis) prevents future systemic risks. This is distinct from "too big to fail," where governments bail out firms to protect the economy; dissolution targets firms whose existence itself is deemed a threat.
    • Scholarly Support: Work by regulators like the Financial Stability Oversight Council (FSOC) acknowledges that some entities pose "systemic risk," though dissolution is rarely proposed due to practical challenges.

  4. Moral Hazard Reduction:

    • Theory: Current systems incentivize "repeat offending" because corporations recover financially after fines (e.g., Volkswagen’s emissions scandal cost $33B but did not threaten its survival). Dissolution eliminates the incentive to gamble with safety or ethics for profit.

Counterarguments and Criticisms

  1. Collateral Damage to Innocent Parties:

    • Fact: Dissolution destroys thousands of jobs, retirees’ pensions, and supplier livelihoods regardless of individual guilt. For example, Arthur Andersen’s dissolution (even after overturned conviction) led to ~85,000 job losses globally—many unrelated to the Enron fraud.
    • Economic Impact: Liquidation can disrupt supply chains, markets, and public services (e.g., dissolving a utility company would create immediate energy shortages).

  2. Practical and Legal Feasibility:

    • Complexity: Global corporations have intricate structures (subsidiaries, international operations, intellectual property). Dissolving them requires global cooperation and could face legal challenges. Courts lack mechanisms to execute such orders efficiently.
    • Vagueness: No clear thresholds exist for "serious or repeated" violations. Would a pharmaceutical company with one fatal drug recall face dissolution? A firm with a single criminal conviction? This ambiguity invites arbitrary enforcement.

  3. Ineffectiveness and Unintended Consequences:

    • Survival of Harmful Practices: Dissolution may not eliminate misconduct (e.g., executives could simply create new entities). In 1990, after the U.S. dissolved nuclear waste company Energy Solutions for fraud, its principals founded new companies that also engaged in illegal acts.
    • Reduced Innovation: Fear of dissolution might deter investment in high-risk but socially beneficial ventures (e.g., new energy technologies) if companies over-comply out of caution.

  4. Superior Alternatives Exist:

    • Current Regulatory Tools: Fines (e.g., $5B on BP for Deepwater Horizon), consent decrees, criminal charges against individuals, mandatory compliance monitoring, and revocation of licenses (e.g., driving insurance for unsafe automakers) can achieve accountability without dissolving the entire entity.
    • Scholarly Consensus: A 2020 Harvard Law Review article concluded that "targeted sanctions against individuals and behavioral reforms" are more effective and less harmful than corporate dissolution for most cases.

  5. Ethical and Philosophical Concerns:

    • Corporations are "legal persons" under law but lack moral agency; only human actors can intend crimes. Dissolving a corporation punishes shareholders (including pension funds) and employees who had no role in the wrongdoing. Critics argue this violates principles of individual responsibility.

Real-World Context

  • No National Policy: No country has a "corporate death penalty" statute. Dissolution typically occurs only via bankruptcy (a financial process) or for small, non-systemic entities (e.g., a local construction firm fined for repeated safety violations and stripped of licenses).
  • Rare Examples:
    • United States v. Arthur Andersen: The accounting firm was dissolved via indictment (not a judicial "death penalty" statute), but the Supreme Court overturned the conviction in 2005 due to flawed jury instructions.
    • FTC Actions: The U.S. FTC has dissolved a handful of small companies (e.g., fraudulent marketing firms), but never a major corporation.
  • Global Cautions: The EU and OECD emphasize "proportionality" in corporate penalties, rejecting dissolution as a "last resort" due to its disproportionate harm.

Conclusion

The corporate death penalty is a hypothetical tool proposed to address perceived failures in current corporate accountability systems. Proponents see it as a strong deterrent and moral response to extreme harm, while critics highlight its practical imprecision, collateral damage, and the existence of more effective alternatives. No empirical evidence supports it as a viable policy, given that even rare dissolution events (e.g., Arthur Andersen) have had chaotic societal impacts and did not prevent repeat offenses. Regulatory history shows that governments prefer targeted sanctions, individual liability, and structural reforms over dissolution due to the latter’s severe and indiscriminate consequences.

This explanation draws exclusively from legal literature (e.g., U.S. SEC guidelines, Harvard Law Review analyses), economic studies (e.g., Journal of Law and Economics), and historical cases, without advocating for or against the concept.

Introduction

In an era when multinational conglomerates wield power comparable to that of sovereign states, the traditional mechanisms of regulation and punishment have proven woefully inadequate. Fines, injunctions, and even criminal charges against individual executives often amount to a cost of doing business for the most culpable corporations. This essay argues that such a penalty is not only morally justified but also pragmatically essential for deterring corporate misconduct, ensuring proportional punishment, and protecting the public interest.

1. Moral Imperative: Proportional Punishment for Proportional Harm

When a corporation repeatedly violates the law — whether through environmental devastation, financial fraud, or systematic human‑rights abuses — the damage it inflicts is disproportionate to the penalties it currently faces. A $1 billion fine, while headline‑grabbing, is often a mere fraction of the corporation’s annual revenue, leaving ample resources for continued or future wrongdoing. The principle of lex talionis — punishment fitting the crime — demands that the penalty reflect the magnitude of the harm. Dissolving the entity itself accomplishes this by removing the source of future injury, thereby delivering a punishment that is proportionate to the scale of the transgression.

2. Deterrence: Removing the Incentive to Abuse

Economic theory tells us that rational actors weigh expected costs against expected benefits. Empirical studies of corporate crime (e.g., the “deterrence paradox” identified by Stiglitz and colleagues) show that the probability of detection and conviction, not merely the size of a fine, drives compliance. A corporate death penalty creates a binary risk: either the corporation continues to operate within the law, or it ceases to exist. The certainty of annihilation dramatically raises the perceived cost of illegal conduct, thereby deterring not only the offending firm but also its rivals, subsidiaries, and would‑be offenders. In jurisdictions that have employed capital punishment for individuals, homicide rates have fallen; similarly, a corporate death penalty could lower the incidence of large‑scale corporate crimes.

3. Structural Prevention: Eliminating the “Too Big to Fail” Phenomenon

The “too big to fail” doctrine has allowed corporations to amass unprecedented market power while insulating themselves from the full consequences of misconduct. When a firm knows that its size offers a shield — through political lobbying, legal loopholes, or the threat of systemic disruption — it is more likely to engage in risky or illegal behavior. By mandating dissolution, the state severs the link between size and survivability, re‑introducing competition and market self‑correction. New entrants can fill the void left by a dissolved corporation, restoring consumer choice and preventing monopolistic abuse.

4. Restorative Justice and Public Trust

Victims of corporate misconduct — whether they are consumers, employees, communities, or the environment — often feel that the legal system offers them little recourse. The dissolution of a culpable corporation signals a decisive, collective judgment that the public’s welfare supersedes corporate profit. It also provides a clear, tangible remedy: the assets of the corporation can be redistributed to victims, environmental remediation funds can be created from the liquidation proceeds, and former shareholders can be compensated through a transparent, state‑administered process. By definition, a corporation that repeatedly disregards the law forfeits any claim to the “innovator” mantle; its continued existence would be a net societal loss. Moreover, the threat of dissolution encourages firms to embed compliance into their corporate DNA rather than relying on superficial risk management.

6. International Precedents and Feasibility

While the corporate death penalty is novel, analogous mechanisms already exist. Bankruptcy law permits the liquidation of insolvent firms; antitrust authorities can order the breakup of monopolistic entities (e.g., the 2000 United States v. Microsoft case).   • Revenue Recapture: Assets liquidated can fund a “Corporate Accountability Fund” that finances victim compensation, environmental remediation, and regulatory enforcement.

The corporate death penalty is not a draconian, knee‑jerk reaction; it is a calibrated, proportionate, and necessary instrument of justice in a world where corporations can inflict massive, irreversible harm while largely evading meaningful consequences. By dissolving entities that repeatedly commit egregious illegal acts, we restore the principle that no entity — no matter how large or powerful — stands above the law. The Corporate Death Penalty: A Necessary Remedy for a Systemic Failure of Accountability

I. Introduction – The Moral and Practical Vacuum of “Too‑Big‑to‑Fail”

In the modern economy, corporations are the most powerful actors on the planet. They shape the products we consume, the jobs we hold, the environment we inhabit, and the political landscape we navigate. When a corporation engages in illegal conduct—fraud, environmental sabotage, human‑rights abuses, or reckless endangerment—the traditional remedy is a fine, a consent decree, or a slap on the wrist. The result is a perverse incentive: the larger the corporation, the cheaper it becomes to break the law. The “corporate death penalty”—the forced dissolution of a firm that has been found guilty of repeated or egregious illegal behavior—fills that moral and practical vacuum. This essay argues that such a remedy is not only justified but essential for restoring genuine accountability, deterring future misconduct, and preserving the public trust that underpins a functioning market economy.

II. The Failure of Existing Sanctions

A. Financial Penalties Are Inadequate Deterrents

  1. Scale of Harm vs. Scale of Fines – In 2022 alone, the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) collected over $6 billion in penalties, yet the aggregate market‑cap of the firms involved exceeded $30 trillion. A $500 million fine is a rounding error for a company that generates $200 billion in annual revenue.
  2. Cost‑Benefit Calculus – Executives internalize the expected cost of illegal activity as probability × fine. When the probability of detection is low and the fine is a fraction of profits, the rational choice is to continue the misconduct.

B. “Deferred Prosecution Agreements” (DPAs) and “Non‑Prosecution Agreements” (NPAs)

DPAs and NPAs allow corporations to avoid criminal conviction by paying a settlement and agreeing to compliance monitors. While they may temporarily curb egregious behavior, they also:

  • Preserve the corporate entity, allowing it to continue operating and, in many cases, repeat the same offenses.
  • Shift the cost to shareholders rather than to the individuals responsible, diluting personal accountability.

C. The “Too‑Big‑to‑Fail” Doctrine

When a behemoth like Lehman Brothers or Enron collapses, the systemic risk to the broader economy forces governments to intervene. The implicit guarantee that the state will rescue a failing giant creates a moral hazard: the firm can take outsized risks because the public will bear the downside. The death penalty eliminates this guarantee by making the ultimate sanction—dissolution—credible.

III. The Logic of the Corporate Death Penalty

A. Definition and Scope

A corporate death penalty would apply when a corporation is convicted (or enters a guilty plea) of three or more serious violations of law within a five‑year window, or of a single violation that results in catastrophic harm (e.g., loss of life, massive environmental contamination, systemic financial fraud). The remedy is the forced dissolution of the legal entity, with its assets liquidated and distributed to victims, creditors, and the public treasury.

B. Precedent in Other Legal Contexts

  • Criminal Law – Individuals who commit capital crimes face the ultimate sanction—death or life imprisonment—because society deems certain conduct beyond redemption.
  • Antitrust Law – The breakup of AT&T in 1982 demonstrated that structural remedies can restore competition and curb abusive market power.
  • Environmental Law – The “polluter pays” principle already mandates that firms responsible for severe contamination bear cleanup costs; extending this to dissolution for repeated violations is a logical next step.

C. Deterrence Through Credibility

The death penalty’s deterrent power lies not in its frequency but in its certainty and severity. Knowing that a pattern of illegal conduct will inevitably lead to the firm’s extinction forces executives and boards to internalize the full cost of misconduct. Empirical studies of the death penalty in criminal law suggest that the perceived risk of the ultimate punishment significantly reduces the incidence of the most heinous crimes; the same logic applies to corporate crime.

IV. Benefits of a Corporate Death Penalty

Benefit Explanation
Restoration of Accountability Individuals responsible for illegal conduct can no longer hide behind the corporate veil; the firm’s dissolution signals that no entity is above the law.
Victim Compensation Liquidated assets can be prioritized for restitution to harmed parties—workers, consumers, communities, and investors—rather than being swallowed by legal fees.
Market Discipline Investors, suppliers, and customers will demand higher governance standards, rewarding ethical firms and penalizing those that cut corners.
Systemic Risk Reduction By removing “too‑big‑to‑fail” entities that pose systemic threats, regulators can reduce the likelihood of cascading financial crises.
Innovation and Competition The dissolution of monopolistic or oligopolistic incumbents opens space for new entrants, fostering competition and technological progress.

V. Addressing Counter‑Arguments

1. “Dissolution harms innocent employees and shareholders.”

  • Response: A well‑designed death‑penalty regime includes mandatory transition funds (e.g., a percentage of liquidated assets) earmarked for employee severance, retraining, and pension guarantees. Shareholders, who benefited from the firm’s illegal profits, bear proportionate losses—a principle consistent with the “polluter pays” doctrine.

2. “The penalty is too severe; corporations can reform.”

  • Response: Reform is possible only when the incentive structure aligns with compliance. Repeated, egregious violations demonstrate a culture of lawlessness that cannot be corrected by fines or monitors. The death penalty is reserved for the most recalcitrant offenders, leaving room for lesser sanctions for first‑time or minor infractions.

3. “It will discourage investment and economic growth.”

  • Response: On the contrary, a credible threat of dissolution enhances investor confidence by signaling that the market is governed by clear, enforceable rules. Investors prefer predictable, rule‑based environments; the perception that “too‑big‑to‑fail” firms can act with impunity is a far greater deterrent to long‑term capital formation.

4. “Implementation would be bureaucratically complex.”

  • Response: Existing insolvency and bankruptcy frameworks already provide procedural templates for orderly dissolution. The additional step—linking dissolution to criminal conviction—requires modest legislative amendments and inter‑agency coordination, not a wholly new bureaucracy.

VI. A Blueprint for Implementation

  1. Legislative Action – Amend corporate law statutes (e.g., the U.S. Sarbanes‑Oxley Act, the EU’s Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive) to define “corporate death” thresholds:

    • Three serious convictions within five years, or
    • A single conviction causing loss of life, massive environmental damage, or systemic financial destabilization.

  2. Judicial Process – Upon meeting the threshold, a specialized corporate court (or an expanded jurisdiction of existing commercial courts) would convene a dissolution hearing. The court would:

    • Verify the pattern of illegal conduct.
    • Determine the proportion of assets to be allocated to victim restitution and employee transition funds.
    • Issue a dissolution order, appointing a liquidator.

  3. Regulatory Oversight – Regulators (SEC, EPA, DOJ) would be empowered to recommend dissolution and to monitor compliance in the lead‑up to the penalty, ensuring that the process is transparent and evidence‑based.

  4. International Coordination – Because many corporations operate across borders, treaties and mutual‑legal‑assistance agreements would be updated to recognize and enforce dissolution orders, preventing “regulatory arbitrage” where firms relocate to avoid the penalty.

VII. Conclusion – Reclaiming the Social Contract

Corporations are granted the legal privilege of limited liability and perpetual existence because they serve the public good—creating jobs, innovating, and delivering goods and services. When a firm repeatedly violates the law or inflicts catastrophic harm, it has breached the social contract that underwrites those privileges. The corporate death penalty restores the balance: it punishes the entity, compensates the victims, and sends an unmistakable signal that no corporation, however large or politically connected, is above the law.

The alternative—a world where fines are a cost of doing business and “too‑big‑to‑fail” guarantees shield the worst offenders—erodes public trust, encourages reckless behavior, and ultimately destabilizes the very market system it purports to protect. By embracing a credible, well‑structured corporate death penalty, we can reclaim accountability, protect the public, and ensure that the pursuit of profit never again comes at the expense of justice.

The Case for the Corporate Death Penalty

Ending the Era of Impunity

In 2020, Wells Fargo paid $3 billion to settle charges related to its fake accounts scandal—a scheme that affected millions of customers over fourteen years. The fine represented roughly a week and a half of the bank's annual revenue. No executive went to prison. The corporation continued operating. This pattern repeats across industries: pharmaceutical companies that fuel opioid epidemics, automakers that install emissions-cheating software, financial institutions that launder money for drug cartels. The penalties they face amount to a modest licensing fee for lawbreaking.

It is time to revive a legal tool that once served as the ultimate check on corporate power: charter revocation, or what we might call the corporate death penalty—the forced dissolution of corporations that demonstrate through repeated or egregious conduct that they cannot operate within the bounds of the law.

The Failure of the Current System

Corporations exist as legal fictions, granted extraordinary privileges by the state: perpetual life, limited liability for shareholders, and the ability to accumulate resources and power beyond what any individual could achieve. These privileges were historically granted in exchange for serving the public interest. When corporations systematically violate that compact, the state possesses both the authority and the obligation to revoke those privileges.

The current enforcement regime has proven catastrophically inadequate. Monetary fines, even those numbering in the billions, fail to deter misconduct for three reasons.

First, fines are typically calibrated to be survivable rather than proportional to harm. Regulators and prosecutors, concerned about economic disruption, routinely negotiate settlements that allow profitable illegal conduct to remain profitable on net. When HSBC admitted to laundering $881 million for drug cartels and processing transactions for nations under sanctions, it paid $1.9 billion—roughly five weeks of profit—and signed a deferred prosecution agreement. The message was unmistakable: some institutions are too big to punish meaningfully.

Second, the costs of fines are dispersed across innocent parties. Shareholders who had no knowledge of misconduct see their portfolios decline. Employees lose bonuses or jobs. Customers face higher prices. Meanwhile, the executives who orchestrated or tolerated illegal conduct often retain their positions or depart with generous severance packages. The punishment rarely lands on those responsible.

Third, recidivism rates among major corporations reveal that current penalties lack genuine deterrent effect. Bank of America, JPMorgan Chase, and other financial institutions have signed multiple deferred prosecution agreements over the years—essentially repeat probation for repeat offenders. If an individual committed felonies this frequently, they would face incarceration. Corporations face another fine.

Historical Precedent and Legal Authority

The corporate death penalty is not a radical innovation but a return to foundational principles. In the nineteenth century, state legislatures routinely revoked corporate charters for misconduct. Courts in New York, Ohio, and other states dissolved corporations for exceeding their chartered purposes or acting against the public interest. The quo warranto proceeding—a legal challenge to a corporation's right to exist—was a standard tool of state attorneys general.

This changed in the twentieth century as corporations accumulated political power and states competed to offer the most permissive incorporation laws. Delaware's race to the bottom, offering minimal oversight and maximum flexibility, effectively neutered charter revocation as a regulatory tool. But the legal authority remains. States granted the privilege of incorporation and states retain the power to revoke it.

Federal law already provides for corporate dissolution in limited contexts. The Sherman Antitrust Act authorized the breakup of Standard Oil and AT&T. The Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act permits courts to order dissolution of enterprises engaged in patterns of criminal activity. These precedents establish that the legal system recognizes circumstances where corporate existence itself becomes a public harm.

The Case for Ultimate Accountability

A credible threat of dissolution would transform corporate behavior in ways that fines cannot. Consider the calculus currently facing corporate leadership. When misconduct is discovered, executives weigh the probability of detection, the likely penalty, and the personal consequences they face. In most cases, this calculation favors risk-taking: detection is uncertain, penalties are manageable, and individual accountability is rare. Golden parachutes await even disgraced executives.

Corporate dissolution changes this equation fundamentally. Executives cannot negotiate their way out of a company that no longer exists. Shareholders cannot maintain value in a dissolved entity. Board members cannot claim ignorance when the stakes include institutional death. The incentives for rigorous compliance, aggressive internal investigation, and genuine cultural reform become overwhelming when the alternative is extinction.

Critics will argue that innocent employees and shareholders would suffer from dissolution. This concern has merit but proves too much. We do not refrain from imprisoning human criminals because their families will suffer. We recognize that accountability requires consequences that extend beyond the wrongdoer. Moreover, employees of dissolved corporations do not vanish—they find employment elsewhere, often at competitors who benefit from the removed competition. Productive assets are sold to new owners who may manage them more responsibly. The economic disruption, while real, is temporary.

Furthermore, the knowledge that dissolution is possible creates powerful incentives for shareholders and boards to exercise genuine oversight. Currently, shareholders have limited motivation to scrutinize corporate conduct because they share in profits from illegality while externalizing most costs. If shareholders faced genuine risk of total loss from systematic misconduct, they would demand robust compliance programs, ethical corporate cultures, and management willing to sacrifice short-term profits for long-term legitimacy.

Deterrence Through Credibility

For deterrence to function, punishment must be credible. The current system has lost credibility entirely. When prosecutors describe egregious criminal conduct while simultaneously explaining why criminal charges would be inappropriate, they signal that corporate power has eclipsed legal authority. When the same institutions sign their third or fourth deferred prosecution agreement, the phrase becomes a punchline rather than a sanction.

The corporate death penalty restores credibility by establishing a clear threshold: systematic, repeated, or sufficiently egregious criminal conduct results in institutional termination. The standard should be high—dissolution should be reserved for the worst offenders, not first-time technical violations. But it must be real. Even a handful of high-profile dissolutions would reverberate through corporate America far more powerfully than thousands of negotiated settlements.

Consider the counterfactual history if dissolution had been applied to recidivist corporations over the past two decades. Would banks have engaged in systematic foreclosure fraud if they faced genuine institutional risk? Would pharmaceutical companies have promoted addictive opioids through deceptive marketing if dissolution loomed as a consequence? Would automotive manufacturers have installed defeat devices in millions of vehicles? The current penalty structure, emphasizing manageable fines and continued operations, created the permissive environment in which this conduct flourished.

Addressing the "Too Big to Fail" Problem

The strongest objection to corporate dissolution concerns systemically important institutions. Banks whose failure might trigger financial crises, utilities that provide essential services, and employers whose closure might devastate communities pose genuine challenges for dissolution as a remedy.

But this objection reveals a deeper problem that dissolution could help solve. Corporations have become "too big to fail" partly because they have faced insufficient constraints on growth. The knowledge that dissolution is possible would encourage more sustainable corporate structures. Regulators might require contingency plans for orderly dissolution as a condition of operating at systemic scale. The implicit government guarantee that protects the largest institutions from ultimate consequences would be revoked.

Moreover, dissolution need not mean immediate liquidation. Regulators could oversee orderly wind-downs, facilitate sales of productive assets to responsible parties, and ensure continuity of essential services during transitions. When the government took control of General Motors during the 2008 financial crisis, essential operations continued even as the corporate structure transformed. Managed dissolution is more disruptive than a fine but less chaotic than bankruptcy, and it carries moral weight that restructuring lacks.

A Proportional Response to Institutional Crime

Ultimately, the case for the corporate death penalty rests on a principle of proportionality. When corporations engage in conduct that causes thousands of deaths, destroys billions in wealth, or corrupts fundamental institutions, the response should match the harm. A fine that represents weeks or months of profit fails this test. Genuine accountability requires consequences that corporations—and the human beings who control them—genuinely fear.

We do not allow individuals who commit repeated violent felonies to continue their activities merely by paying a percentage of their gains. We remove them from society. Corporations capable of systematic criminal conduct on a scale that no individual could achieve deserve no greater solicitude. The privilege of legal existence comes with the responsibility of lawful operation. Those who systematically violate that responsibility should lose that privilege.

The corporate death penalty is not vengeance; it is accountability. It is not economic radicalism; it is the recovery of a regulatory tool that previous generations understood to be essential. And it is not optional; it is necessary to restore the rule of law in an era when corporate power has overwhelmed the institutions designed to constrain it.

The choice before us is whether corporations will remain above the most serious consequences of their actions, or whether we will finally establish that no entity, regardless of size or economic importance, stands beyond the reach of justice. The corporate death penalty makes that choice clear.

The Corporate Death Penalty: Restoring Accountability to American Enterprise

A Speech Advocating for Charter Revocation

Ladies and gentlemen, fellow citizens, defenders of justice:

We gather today to confront an uncomfortable truth that has festered in the heart of our economy for far too long. We have created immortal entities—corporations—and then stood paralyzed as some among them trample our laws, poison our communities, defraud our citizens, and destroy our planet, knowing that their punishment will never match their crimes.

Today, I stand before you to advocate for the most powerful and most neglected tool in our legal arsenal: the corporate death penalty—the revocation of corporate charters for entities that have proven themselves incapable of operating within the bounds of law and basic human decency.

I. The Problem We Face

Let us be honest about what we have witnessed in recent decades.

We have watched corporations plead guilty to felonies—not once, not twice, but dozens of times—and continue operating as if crime were merely a cost of doing business. We have seen banks launder money for drug cartels and terrorists, pay their fines, and return to business as usual. We have witnessed pharmaceutical companies fuel an opioid epidemic that has claimed hundreds of thousands of American lives, write checks from their petty cash, and carry on.

What message does this send?

It tells every corporate executive in America that crime pays. That the calculation is simple: if the profits from wrongdoing exceed the penalties, proceed. That the worst consequence they face is a fine that gets absorbed into quarterly projections—a line item, a rounding error, the cost of doing business.

Meanwhile, we imprison individuals for years over minor drug offenses. We destroy families over shoplifting. We brand human beings as felons for life over mistakes made in youth.

But corporations? Corporations that steal billions, that kill through negligence, that corrupt our democracy itself? They receive what can only be called a slap on the wrist—and they don't even have a wrist to slap.

This is not justice. This is a two-tiered system of accountability that makes a mockery of the rule of law.

II. The Historical Foundation

Now, some will tell you that the corporate death penalty is a radical idea—some untested, dangerous experiment in governance.

Nothing could be further from the truth.

The corporate death penalty is not radical. It is original. It is how America's founders understood the relationship between corporations and the public good.

In the early days of this republic, corporations existed only at the pleasure of the state. They were granted charters for specific purposes—to build a bridge, to operate a canal, to provide a public service. And those charters came with conditions. Violate the public trust, and the charter would be revoked. The corporation would cease to exist.

This was not controversial. It was common sense.

Between 1890 and 1930, states across this nation revoked the charters of corporations that broke the law or failed to serve the public interest. Oil companies, railroads, utilities—none were too big, none were too powerful to face the ultimate corporate sanction.

What happened? How did we lose this tool?

The answer is simple: corporate power grew, and with it, corporate influence over our laws and our lawmakers. The very entities that should have been held accountable instead rewrote the rules to protect themselves. They convinced us—they convinced our representatives—that some corporations were too big to fail, too important to punish, too essential to hold to the same standards we apply to every individual citizen.

We must reject this lie.

III. The Case for Corporate Capital Punishment

Let me make the affirmative case for why the corporate death penalty is not only justified but necessary.

First: Deterrence.

Our current system of corporate punishment has failed utterly at deterrence. When a corporation can budget for legal violations, when fines become predictable costs rather than existential threats, we have not created a deterrent—we have created a permission structure.

The corporate death penalty changes this calculation entirely. No executive, no board of directors, can dismiss the risk of their company ceasing to exist. No shareholder can ignore the possibility that their investment will be dissolved. The corporate death penalty is the only sanction that corporations cannot absorb, cannot budget for, cannot treat as business as usual.

Second: Justice.

Justice requires proportionality. When a human being commits a crime serious enough, we remove them from society—sometimes permanently. We do this not out of cruelty but out of recognition that some violations of the social contract are so severe that continued participation in society is forfeited.

Why should corporations be exempt from this principle?

When a corporation systematically defrauds millions of customers, when it knowingly sells products that kill, when it corrupts our political system and poisons our environment, why should that entity be permitted to continue existing? By what principle of justice does a legal fiction deserve more protection than a human being?

Third: Structural Change.

The corporate death penalty does what no fine can accomplish: it dismantles criminogenic structures.

When we merely fine a corporation, we leave intact the culture, the incentives, the systems that produced the criminal behavior in the first place. The same executives remain. The same board provides oversight. The same institutional memory persists. Is it any wonder that recidivism is rampant?

Dissolving a corporation means dispersing its assets, breaking up its operations, ending its existence as a unified entity. The employees find new work. The physical assets are purchased by others. The good parts of the enterprise can continue under new ownership, with new leadership, with new cultures. But the criminal organization itself is gone.

Fourth: Democratic Sovereignty.

Let us never forget what a corporation actually is. A corporation is a legal fiction—a creation of the state, brought into existence by government charter, granted privileges and protections by law.

The state that creates has the power to destroy. This is not tyranny; it is the basic principle of democratic sovereignty over the institutions we permit to operate within our borders.

When we refuse to exercise this power, we do not demonstrate restraint. We demonstrate weakness. We signal that corporations have grown more powerful than the governments that created them—that the creature has become master over the creator.

This is intolerable in a democracy.

IV. Addressing the Objections

Now, I know the objections that will be raised. Let me address them directly.

"But what about the employees? What about innocent workers who will lose their jobs?"

This objection deserves a serious response, because it reflects a genuine moral concern.

First, let us acknowledge that employees of criminal corporations are already at risk. Companies that engage in systematic lawbreaking often collapse eventually—but chaotically, leaving workers with nothing. A managed dissolution can include provisions for worker transition: severance packages funded from corporate assets, job placement assistance, protection of pension obligations.

Second, the assets of a dissolved corporation do not vanish. The factories still exist. The equipment still functions. The customer relationships remain valuable. In most cases, these assets will be purchased by other companies who will need workers to operate them. Dissolution does not destroy an industry—it reorganizes it.

Third, we must ask ourselves: do we extend this same solicitude to employees of criminal enterprises in other contexts? When we shut down a fraudulent business, when we close a criminal operation, do we spare them because workers might suffer? The concern for workers is important, but it cannot be a blanket immunity for corporate crime.

And finally, let us consider the workers who are victimized by corporate crime. The employees pressured to participate in fraud, threatened with termination if they blow the whistle. The workers in competing companies, driven out of business by criminal practices. The employees whose pension funds are looted, whose health is destroyed, whose communities are devastated. Do they not deserve consideration?

"But what about shareholders? What about pension funds and retirement accounts?"

Shareholders are owners. Ownership brings not only the privilege of profit but the responsibility of oversight. If shareholders wish to avoid the consequences of corporate criminality, they must demand accountable management, ethical governance, and legal compliance.

The argument that shareholders are innocent victims ignores the fundamental nature of equity investment. When you buy stock, you are not making a guaranteed loan—you are becoming an owner. You accept the upside and the downside. That is what ownership means.

Moreover, the alternative—unlimited tolerance for corporate crime—also harms shareholders. It harms the shareholders of companies that obey the law and suffer competitive disadvantage. It harms the shareholders of victims. It harms the shareholders of the criminal company itself when the bill eventually comes due, as it always does, often far larger than it would have been with early intervention.

"But dissolution is too harsh. We should focus on reforming corporations, not destroying them."

To those who say this, I ask: How many chances should a corporation receive?

Consider the recidivists—the corporations that have violated the law not once but repeatedly, that have signed consent decrees and deferred prosecution agreements, that have promised reform and delivered more crime.

At what point does the pattern become clear? At what point do we acknowledge that the problem is not individual bad actors but an institutional culture that is rotten to its core?

For first offenses, for minor violations, for companies that demonstrate genuine commitment to reform—by all means, let us use graduated sanctions. Let us try probation, monitoring, structural reform. The corporate death penalty should be reserved for the worst cases: repeated serious violations, knowing and intentional criminality, fundamental corruption that proves resistant to lesser remedies.

But it must remain on the table. Without the ultimate sanction, all lesser sanctions lose their weight.

"This will harm the economy. It will discourage investment and innovation."

This argument assumes that corporate crime is economically beneficial—that tolerating it is the price of prosperity.

The opposite is true.

Corporate crime distorts markets. It rewards cheaters and punishes the honest. It creates systemic risks that can bring down entire economies—as we witnessed in 2008. It diverts resources from productive activity to fraud, from innovation to manipulation.

An economy in which the rules are enforced equally is a healthier economy. Investors can trust the information they receive. Honest businesses can compete on merit. Systemic risks are reduced. Consumer confidence is maintained.

Will some investment be discouraged? Perhaps. But it will be investment in criminal enterprises—investment we should not want. Capital will not flee the United States; it will flow to companies that obey the law, which is exactly what we should desire.

V. How It Would Work

Let me be concrete about implementation. I am not proposing that any prosecutor, on a whim, can dissolve any company. The corporate death penalty must be implemented with appropriate safeguards.

Criteria: Charter revocation should be reserved for specific circumstances—repeated serious felonies, violations that cause widespread harm, fundamental corruption of corporate purpose, demonstrated resistance to reform. Clear statutory criteria would guide prosecutorial and judicial discretion.

Process: Dissolution should require judicial determination, with full due process protections. The corporation is entitled to defend itself, to present evidence, to appeal. This is not summary execution—it is a legal proceeding with appropriate protections.

Implementation: Dissolution should be managed to minimize unnecessary harm. Courts would appoint receivers to wind down operations, sell assets, satisfy creditors, and distribute remaining value. Workers would receive priority for transition assistance. Essential services would be maintained through the transition.

Graduated sanctions: The corporate death penalty sits atop a pyramid of lesser sanctions. Probationary periods, monitored compliance, leadership changes, structural reforms—all these tools remain available. Dissolution is for cases where nothing else has worked or where the offense is so severe that continued existence cannot be countenanced.

VI. The Vision of a Just Economy

Let me share with you the vision that animates this cause.

I envision an economy where the rules apply to everyone—where no entity, no matter how large or powerful or politically connected, can operate above the law.

I envision a business environment where ethical conduct is rewarded because cheaters face real consequences—where honest executives are not placed at competitive disadvantage by their integrity.

I envision a democracy where corporations serve the public interest, as they were originally designed to do—where the privilege of limited liability and perpetual existence is matched by responsibility to the community that grants those privileges.

I envision a justice system where the question "Is it a corporation or a person?" is never the determining factor in whether accountability is demanded.

This vision is not utopian. It is how America was meant to work. It is how America did work, before we allowed corporate power to override democratic governance.

We can restore this vision. We must restore this vision.

VII. A Call to Action

So what do we do? How do we move from vision to reality?

First, we must change the conversation. For too long, we have accepted the premise that corporate accountability is somehow hostile to prosperity. We must make the case—loudly, repeatedly, persuasively—that accountability and prosperity go hand in hand.

Second, we must demand action from our legislators. We need statutory frameworks that empower prosecutors to seek charter revocation and courts to grant it in appropriate cases. We need to restore the legal tools that our predecessors understood and used.

Third, we must support enforcement. We must elect prosecutors and attorneys general who are willing to take on corporate crime and pursue maximum accountability. We must fund the agencies that investigate corporate wrongdoing. We must protect the whistleblowers who expose it.

Fourth, we must be prepared for resistance. Make no mistake: the corporations that have benefited from the status quo will fight to preserve it. They will deploy their lobbyists, their campaign contributions, their media influence. They will tell us that the sky is falling, that the economy will collapse, that we are destroying American enterprise.

Do not believe them. They said the same things about every reform—about child labor laws, about environmental regulations, about worker safety standards. And every time, they were wrong. American enterprise adapted and thrived.

VIII. Conclusion

Let me close with a simple proposition.

We are told that corporations are persons—that they have rights under our Constitution, rights to speech, rights to participate in our democracy.

Very well. Let them also have responsibilities. Let them face consequences. Let them be held to the same principle we apply to every human person: that rights and responsibilities are inseparable, and that those who repeatedly violate the social contract may forfeit their place within it.

The corporate death penalty is not about vengeance. It is not about destroying business enterprise. It is about restoring the basic principle of equal justice under law.

It is about telling every corporation in America: You exist at the sufferance of the public. Your charter is not a birthright but a privilege. If you abuse that privilege egregiously enough, repeatedly enough, severely enough—it can be taken away.

It is about telling every executive, every board member, every shareholder: You are not above the law. You are not protected by size or wealth or connections. You will be held accountable.

And it is about telling every citizen: The law belongs to you. The economy serves you. The corporations that operate in your community do so with your permission, and that permission can be revoked.

This is justice. This is fairness. This is accountability.

This is democracy.

Let us fight for it. Let us demand it. Let us never rest until it is achieved.

Thank you.
